source.title: Neural Dynamics as the Composition of Quantized Units
source.authors: J. Minniti; Aravinth Kulanthaivelu; Richard Sproat

record.tranche_reason: The study measures held-out loss across parameter and data scales in a controlled synthetic task, rather than reproducing language-model scaling experiments. Its results also examine whether fitted scaling exponents remain stable across fit windows.
record.gate_note: The empirical scaling results are from hierarchical sparse parity (HSP) models, not language models. The text's statements about prior scaling-law studies are citations, not results from this study. Q-model and Q-guided-training accuracy results do not measure a claim version here.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a quanta-acquisition theory of scaling and demonstrates it on hierarchical sparse parity (HSP), a synthetic Boolean task trained with MLPs. The demand law that produces the power law is imposed on purpose by the data generator (Appendix C: closure demands are prescribed by depth). The scaling fits therefore check the theory's predicted exponent in an engineered toy. They do not test whether power-law loss arises in language-model pretraining or in other natural modalities and regimes. The authors state the work does not test natural language or LLMs. No version is tested; the findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that, under assumptions about quanta demand and poset geometry, staggered discrete acquisitions give smooth loss and parameter/data scaling regimes in HSP. They caution that data fits are window-sensitive and that validation across seeds, architectures, resource ranges and distributions is needed. The paraphrase omits the paper's other main results: Q-model recovery from a Number Naming Transformer, and Q-guided training raising accuracy from 84.9% to 94.7%.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled hierarchical sparse parity tasks and task-conditioned ReLU MLPs, rather than language-model pretraining runs. It fits parameter and data scaling separately and does not test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The data-scaling exponent changes across earlier and later fit windows; the text also reports trajectory instability and endpoint-selection sensitivity.

fits_no_version.finding: In HSP with a generator-imposed depth–demand law, MLP held-out loss vs parameters follows power laws whose fitted exponents are within 1.4–5.7% of the prescribed α (R² ≈ 0.89).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In synthetic tasks with an imposed power-law skill demand, the parameter-scaling exponent of loss matches the demand exponent α.

fits_no_version.finding: Online data scaling in HSP roughly matches the predicted slope α/(1+α), with 9.9–26.7% error over a post-hoc selected central window.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quanta-demand theory predicts data-scaling exponents α/(1+α) in engineered compositional tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Splitting each data-fit window at its geometric mean gives a smaller later-half slope in all three arms (e.g. 0.4339 vs 0.1164). A high full-window R² does not establish a stationary exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finite-window data-scaling exponents in toy compositional tasks are non-stationary and sensitive to window choice.

record.problems: The scaling experiments use a controlled synthetic HSP task and MLPs, not large language models. The data-scaling trajectories have plateaus and instability, and their fitted slopes vary substantially with the selected window. The paper itself calls for broader validation across seeds, architectures, resource ranges, and data distributions.

untested.parts: All: no language-model pretraining loss and no compute scaling.
All: no extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
All: no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not studied. The synthetic HSP power law is engineered by the generator.
No comparison of published laws, parameter-counting, schedule or fitting-method effects in language models. The only window sensitivity shown is in an engineered toy.

missing.what: Parameter-sweep checkpoint selection and stability: late muP-related instabilities (models forget, then recover tasks). The α=0.339 fit uses the last stable checkpoint in a post-hoc 18–20M window. Late common-checkpoint fits keep R² ≈ 0.89–0.90.
missing.versions: none (fits_no_version: fit-dependence in toy parameter scaling)

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the rows to V5 and V7. However, the power law is induced by construction: β prescribes α through Möbius-inverted query probabilities. The task is synthetic Boolean parity, not another modality or training regime in V5's sense. The authors state that the work does not test natural language or LLMs. All rows are therefore reassigned to none and no labels are given. A researcher may still view the HSP window-sensitivity result as illustrative for V7.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out pretraining loss in language models, or scaling with compute.
No prediction of much larger runs from fits on smaller runs is reported.
No fixed-compute-budget allocation between parameter count and tokens is tested.
The study does not compare depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The scaling tests use synthetic HSP tasks and MLPs only; they do not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No downstream-task performance relationship with scale or pretraining loss is tested.

The study tests fit-window sensitivity in its HSP data-scaling runs, but not disagreement among language-model scaling studies, compute-optimal allocation, or the effects of alternative parameter-counting methods.

reader_labels.reason: Held-out loss follows fitted power-law trends with exponents close to the prescribed values in this synthetic task (R1–R3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The central-window fits are imperfect and trajectories show plateaus and instability; the authors also note sensitivity to the fitting window (R4–R6).

reader_labels.label: supports
